html:
A Pakistani humanitarian who built the Edhi Foundation, the country's largest welfare network, with the world's largest volunteer ambulance service. He lived from 1928 to 2016.

He was born in Bantva in Gujarat, in British India, to a Memon trading family. At the Partition of India in 1947 his family moved to Karachi. There, moved by the suffering he had seen while caring for his paralysed mother, he opened a small free dispensary in 1951 and began to collect donations in the street.

Over six decades the work grew into ambulances, morgues, homeless shelters, orphanages, homes for the old and the mentally ill, and animal shelters. Edhi and his staff collected and buried unclaimed bodies, and placed cradles outside centres where unwanted babies could be left safely rather than abandoned. His wife Bilquis Edhi ran much of the work for women and children.

He lived very simply, wore the same few clothes and took no government money, relying on public gifts. He refused to divide people by religion or sect. When he died, Pakistan gave him a state funeral.
